# Architecture to Autonomy — Full Content Index for LLMs

Site: https://architecturetoautonomy.com/

## VCF 9.1 is Out. What Does This Mean to You?
URL: https://architecturetoautonomy.com/posts/vcf-9-1-what-does-this-mean-to-you.html
Published: May 6, 2026
Keywords: vcf 9.1, vmware cloud foundation, private cloud, agentic platform, ai infrastructure, gpu pooling, memory tiering, sdn fabric, drift remediation, agent runtime hosting

VCF 9.1 dropped alongside Broadcom's preview of the Private Cloud Outlook 2026, which reports public cloud production AI inference down ~15% year over year while 56% of enterprises now run or plan to run inference in a private cloud. VCF 9.1 is the substrate underneath that shift — the stepping stone to the agentic enterprise platform that follows. The post walks through six concrete situations enterprise platform teams are hitting today and how 9.1 addresses each.

Key arguments:
- Memory headroom: refresh budgets aren't catching up with workload growth. VCF 9.1 introduces memory tiering with NVMe-backed extension so the same host fleet can carry more without a hardware refresh.
- AI capacity planning around GPU count is the wrong axis. 9.1 expands GPU partitioning and pooling so multiple workloads share accelerators with quotas rather than dedicated cards. The right unit of capacity becomes "GPU-hours under policy" not "GPUs per cluster."
- SDN overlay and physical fabric coordination has been a manual handoff. 9.1 gives the SDN layer first-class awareness of the underlying fabric so changes propagate consistently — fewer change-window collisions, fewer wedge states.
- Hosting AI agents requires runtime controls most platforms bolt on. 9.1 has native primitives for agent identity, scoped tool access, and replayable audit trails, so platform teams don't have to staple a separate control plane on top.
- Auditors keep finding the same drift between intended state and running state. 9.1 ships automated drift remediation against a declared baseline, closing the most common audit findings without a separate compliance product.
- Agent data access shouldn't have to leave the controlled estate. 9.1 introduces a governed enterprise data tier with scoped access by agent identity, replacing the typical pattern of agents pulling data from public cloud copies.
- 9.1 is not the agentic platform. It is the substrate. The agentic platform stack (delegation, verification, containment, economics) sits on top, and post-9.1 the substrate is finally ready to carry it.

Recommendations by role:
- Platform owner: the planning question is no longer "do we have GPU capacity?" it's "what's the policy under which our shared GPU pool serves competing workloads?"
- Architect: stop solving agent hosting at the application layer. 9.1 makes it a platform capability — design for it once, get it everywhere.
- Operations: drift remediation as a 9.1 feature kills a class of audit findings. Re-baseline and retire the bolt-on compliance tooling you wrote around the old gap.

Bottom line: VCF 9.1 isn't a feature release; it's the substrate upgrade that makes the agentic enterprise platform plausible to run on-premise. The shift from "GPU shortage panic" to "GPU policy under control" is the directional change underneath the headline.

## The Seam: Where Classical EA Meets Agentic Governance
URL: https://architecturetoautonomy.com/posts/the-seam-classical-ea-meets-agentic-governance.html
Published: April 22, 2026
Keywords: enterprise architecture, agentic systems, TOGAF, Zachman, pace layering, runtime governance, MCP, AI governance, NIST AI RMF, ISO 42001

Classical enterprise architecture frameworks (TOGAF, Zachman, BDAT) assume systems eventually stop changing long enough to finish the diagram. Agentic systems do not rest. There is no to-be state, only a continuously evolving runtime. The gap between architectures you can draw and runtimes you must operate is a framework problem, not an engineering one.

Key arguments:
- Stewart Brand's 1994 shearing layers (Site, Structure, Skin, Services, Space Plan, Stuff) translate directly to agentic systems. Robust systems separate layers by change velocity and let fast layers move without disturbing slow ones.
- A six-layer synthesis for agentic systems: L0 Constitution and Purpose (years — immutable principles, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001), L1 Trust and Identity Fabric (year+ — agent identity distinct from user identity, delegation chains, audit substrate), L2 Capability Contracts (quarters — tool schemas, MCP endpoints, data product interfaces), L3 Cognitive Patterns (months — ReAct, reflection loops, multi-agent topologies), L4 Models and Prompts (weeks — weights, providers, configs), L5 Evaluation and Telemetry (continuous — drift detectors, eval suites, reasoning-trace capture).
- The prime directive: a change in a faster layer must never violate the contracts of a slower one. A prompt rewrite at L4 cannot bypass a tool-scope constraint at L2. Every layer exposes versioned contracts upward and consumes them downward.
- Four operating principles gate every change: Contract-First Implementation-Volatile, Shadow-Before-Promote (parallel eval against real traffic), Reversibility by Default (pinned rollbacks; human confirmation for irreversible actions like outbound payments or SWIFT messages), Runtime Introspection (agents can query their own architecture).
- The seam is the contract surface between the classical EA estate and the agentic substrate. Identity fabric meets agent identity. Service catalog meets tool registry. Data product contracts meet agent data access. Change advisory boards meet deployment promotions. The two sides do not share a clock, so the contracts at the seam must absorb the velocity mismatch.
- Prior art converges on two halves. Sean J. Savage's AI Pace Layers (October 2025) extended Brand to AI product design. MI9 (arXiv 2508.03858) formalised agentic runtime governance in six mechanisms. Gartner named Pace-Layered Application Strategy more than a decade ago for traditional enterprise apps. The join between these is not yet drawn deliberately.
- L5 (evaluation and telemetry) is the weakest layer in practice. Most teams resource it like MLOps plumbing, when it needs to be a runtime layer with authority to gate promotions across every other layer.

Recommendations by role:
- CIO/CTO: stop asking for a to-be architecture for agentic estates. Ask instead what the agentic layers are, what contracts connect them, and what contracts join them to the classical estate.
- Enterprise architect: TOGAF and Zachman handle half the problem. The other half is designing the seam between a deterministic substrate and a continuously evolving runtime.
- Platform engineer: L5 is the work. Evaluation, telemetry, reasoning-trace capture, drift detection. It sounds like MLOps and gets funded like MLOps but it is neither.

Bottom line: for organisations with a mature classical estate running agentic systems on top, the seam is where architectural decisions compound or collapse. Almost nobody is resourcing for it deliberately yet.

## Hardware Is Eating AI: The New Narrative Beyond Software Eating the World
URL: https://architecturetoautonomy.com/posts/hardware-eating-ai-new-narrative.html
Published: April 12, 2026
Keywords: ai infrastructure, hardware, supply chain, enterprise strategy, GPU shortage, HBM, DRAM, NVIDIA, Broadcom, VCF

Marc Andreessen argued software would eat the world because it has near-zero marginal cost. AI inverts that assumption: every inference costs silicon, power, and water. Hardware is now eating AI, and AI is eating everything else.

Key arguments:
- The AI hardware bottleneck is not just GPUs. The binding constraints are HBM memory (70% of global DRAM consumed by AI data centers in 2026), CoWoS advanced packaging (fully allocated through mid-2027), and power infrastructure.
- GPU lead times stretch to 36-52 weeks. NVIDIA cut consumer RTX 5000 production by 30-40% to prioritize data centers. Micron discontinued its consumer Crucial memory line.
- Five forces will break the bottleneck: alternative accelerators (Google TPU, Groq LPU, Arm AGI CPU), model efficiency improvements, processing-in-memory architectures, new fab capacity (online by 2028), and neuromorphic computing.
- NVIDIA paid $20 billion to license Groq's LPU technology, which bypasses HBM entirely using on-chip SRAM — an admission that GPUs are not optimal for inference workloads that now account for over 55% of all AI compute.
- Broadcom plays both sides: custom TPU silicon with Google (through 2031, with 3.5GW of compute capacity for Anthropic) and VMware Cloud Foundation 9.0 for software-defined efficiency (NVMe memory tiering delivers 40:1 cost ratio vs DRAM).
- The shortage creates a "compute divide" between hyperscalers with forward GPU contracts and everyone else.
- The shortage is cyclical, not structural, with meaningful relief arriving by 2028. But strategic choices made during this window will define competitive advantage for a decade.

Enterprise recommendations: diversify compute across chip types, invest in model efficiency, plan procurement in years not quarters, factor energy geography into infrastructure strategy.

## The Agentic Enterprise Needs a New Platform Stack
URL: https://architecturetoautonomy.com/posts/agentic-enterprise-platform-stack.html
Published: March 5, 2026
Keywords: platform architecture, agentic systems, enterprise ai, delegation, verification, containment

A technical blueprint for why SaaS-era architecture assumptions break with autonomous agents and what to build instead.

Key arguments:
- Traditional cloud platforms optimized for human-driven workflows. Agentic systems introduce four missing requirements: delegation (scoped entitlements for agents), verification (replayable audit trails), containment (blast-radius controls for tool access), and economics (budget caps for autonomous spending).
- The platform must answer: what can an agent do, how do you prove what happened, how do you prevent tool access from becoming a breach vector, and how do you control runaway costs.
- Agent autonomy should be treated as a platform capability, not an application feature.
- Architecture is the answer to accountability in autonomous systems.

## Agentic Operating Models for Enterprise Execution
URL: https://architecturetoautonomy.com/posts/agentic-operating-models.html
Published: March 5, 2026
Keywords: operating models, agentic systems, governance, enterprise execution

A practical operating model for enterprise agentic systems covering ownership, controls, lifecycle governance, and measurable outcomes.

Key arguments:
- Agentic pilots stall in production without explicit ownership, autonomy boundaries, and lifecycle accountability.
- Operating models must define who owns the agent, what boundaries govern its autonomy, how its lifecycle is managed, and what measurable outcomes it must deliver.
- Without these structures, enterprises end up with experiments that never scale.

## Leading from Altitude: Why Strategic Distance Drives Better Decisions
URL: https://architecturetoautonomy.com/posts/leading-from-altitude-strategic-distance.html
Published: October 27, 2025
Keywords: leadership, strategy, operating model, burnout, technology leadership

A leadership perspective on strategic distance, inspired by the Himalayas.

Key arguments:
- Over 60% of IT professionals report high burnout levels, climbing higher for leadership roles.
- Physical and mental distance shifts the brain from reactive problem-solving to reflective strategy.
- Resilience demands recovery cycles, innovation needs room to breathe, perspective is a strategic asset, and the AI era demands human renewal.
- Leaders should schedule non-negotiable downtime, cultivate boundaries, change environments to change thinking, and return with renewed intention.

## Whetstone — Free Practice Exams for AI Certifications
URL: https://architecturetoautonomy.com/assets/Tools/whetstone/whetstone.html
Type: Web app (free, browser-based, no account or install)
Keywords: AI certification practice exam, Claude Certified Architect, CCAR-F practice test, AI certification prep, free mock exam, test prep, Whetstone

Whetstone is a free, browser-based practice-exam app for AI certifications, published by Samir Roshan on Architecture to Autonomy. It runs entirely in the browser — no account, no sign-up, no install — and stores your results and missed items locally in your browser only.

The first exam bank covers the Claude Certified Architect – Foundations exam (code CCAR-F), written against the published Exam Guide v1.0 (July 2026). It is unofficial and not affiliated with any certification body; all items are original and contain no real exam content.

Key facts:
- 151 original items covering all six scenarios and all 30 task statements, including 36 contrast pairs where a single detail changes the correct answer.
- Item formats: multiple choice and multiple response; each item states how many responses to select.
- Blueprint-weighted scoring on a 100 to 1,000 scale with 720 to pass — the same scale as the real exam, so a weak high-weight domain costs what it would on the actual test.
- 10 fixed-form timed mock tests (60 items each, 120 minutes), built to blueprint weights, with options reshuffled every attempt and best score stored per test.
- Additional modes: custom-length runs (timed or untimed), whole-bank timed, simulation, untimed study, targeted drills by content domain, and a mode to re-drill items missed before.

Whetstone is aimed at candidates preparing for AI certification exams who want realistic, blueprint-accurate practice that mirrors the real scoring model, without accounts or paywalls.

## A2A Enterprise Agent Plane — Governed Agentic Operations for VCF
URL: https://architecturetoautonomy.com/assets/Tools/agent-plane/
Source: https://github.com/code4freedom/a2a-enterprise-agent-plane
Type: Open reference implementation (Python / FastAPI, self-hosted, Docker supported)
Keywords: agentic operations, VMware Cloud Foundation, VCF, agent control plane, AI governance, policy-governed agents, approval gates, incident operations, auditability

A2A Enterprise Agent Plane, positioned as a VCF Command Center, is a scenario-driven reference implementation of governed AI operations across VMware Cloud Foundation, published by Samir Roshan on Architecture to Autonomy. It is the runnable version of the control-plane pattern argued for on the blog: agent autonomy bounded by explicit policy, identity, and approval gates rather than trust.

The control-plane pattern it implements, in five layers:
- Application: an executive command center and scenario-driven operator workflow.
- Agent control plane: evidence correlation, policy checks, tool routing, approvals, replay, and audit.
- Security: explicit approval gates and governed execution paths.
- Runtime: API service, simulated VCF adapters, and session lifecycle.
- Infrastructure: profile-based deployment, `local` for labs and `vcf` for a stricter production posture.

What it does:
- Seeds a VCF-style estate with workload domains, protected services, and integration fabric health.
- Runs curated executive scenarios for performance, security, and capacity incidents.
- Correlates simulated evidence from VCF Operations, Networks, Logs, SDDC Manager, NSX, Avi, and Automation.
- Generates a governed action plan carrying confidence, blast radius, and rollback hints.
- Auto-executes low-risk actions through simulated fulfillment adapters, and holds higher-risk actions for explicit approval.
- Verifies outcomes and keeps a replayable decision trail for audit.

Important caveat: the project is platform-agnostic by design and ships with mock adapters, so fulfillment is simulated rather than live. The vSphere adapter (pyvmomi) is a deliberate stub. Connecting a nested VCF lab requires replacing the mock implementations with real vSphere, Kubernetes, and ITSM integrations, using config/vcf.yaml as the stricter baseline.

The argument it embodies: enterprises do not adopt agentic operations by making agents more capable, but by making their actions governable. Confidence scores, blast-radius estimates, rollback paths, approval gates, and a replayable audit trail are what let an operator delegate safely.

---

## Neural Seed — Thesis-as-Code Deal Discovery for Solo Investors
URL: https://architecturetoautonomy.com/assets/Tools/neural-seed/
Source: https://github.com/code4freedom/Neural_Seed
Type: Open-source self-hosted application (Apache-2.0, Python 3.12 / FastAPI)
Keywords: deal discovery, angel investing, venture scout, thesis-as-code, AI sourcing, self-hosted, transparent scoring, investment thesis, Claude, pgvector

Neural Seed is a self-hosted AI deal-discovery engine for solo operators - angels, scouts, and sector-focused VCs - published by Samir Roshan on Architecture to Autonomy. Its positioning is thesis-as-code, transparent scoring, and zero data-provider lock-in.

How it works, in four steps:
- Ingests public signals: GitHub trending, Hacker News "Show HN", and user-configured RSS feeds. An in-process scheduler runs GitHub trending daily and Show HN hourly.
- Extracts structured company and founder records from raw posts using Claude with tool-use at temperature=0, storing the prompt hashes alongside each result.
- Scores each company against a Markdown thesis the user controls. It ships with theses/devinfra-v1.md as a worked example, intended to be forked.
- Surfaces a ranked pipeline in a server-rendered web UI, plus a daily brief printed to stdout: the top three companies scoring 7.0 or above in the last 24 hours. (SMTP settings exist in config but mail delivery is not implemented in this phase.)

The central design idea is that the investment thesis is a file rather than a hidden setting. Theses are Markdown with a YAML front-matter block. Scores are keyed on thesis_version = {name}-{version}-{sha256(file)[:8]}, so editing the thesis file automatically produces a new version and prior scores are preserved. Every score is traceable to the exact prompt bytes, the model version, and the source documents that produced it.

Architecture, five stages: Sources (connectors) to Ingestion (scheduler) to Storage (Postgres) to Intelligence (enrichment and scoring) to Surface (api, ui, briefs).

Stack: Python 3.12 with uv, FastAPI + Jinja (server-rendered) + Tailwind, Postgres 16 with pgvector, SQLAlchemy 2.0 async, Alembic, APScheduler in-process, Claude via the anthropic SDK, and Voyage embeddings.

Running it: a demo mode requires no API keys and generates a deterministic synthetic dataset of 52 companies flagged as demo data (cp .env.example .env; docker compose up -d postgres; make install; make demo; open http://localhost:8000). Note the README omits the postgres step, but make install runs Alembic migrations and needs a live database. Full mode requires NEURAL_SEED_DEMO=0, an ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and a GITHUB_TOKEN, plus Postgres via Docker Compose.

Important caveat: Neural Seed ships with no authentication. Its README states explicitly that it should be run on localhost only and must not be exposed to the public internet. It is a single-operator tool. The repo describes itself as a Phase 1 vertical slice and an experimental project; the five scoring axes (market, team, traction, fit, timing) are a fixed set in code, users control their weights and prose rather than the axis names; and the thesis version hash covers the thesis body, so editing only the front-matter does not mint a new version.

## Isvara — Your Agentic Assistant for Private Cloud
URL: https://isvara.io/
Type: Live web app (grounded reading site + agentic co-pilot)
Keywords: private cloud, VMware Cloud Foundation, vSphere, agentic assistant, grounded answers, operations guide, iO, VCF operations

Isvara is a co-pilot for enterprise private cloud, built by Samir Roshan. Its own description: read the guide, ask iO, and score your operations — answers cite the guide and relevant knowledge references.

- The site presents a five-part private cloud operations guide as a first-class reading experience.
- iO is the agentic assistant: it answers operational questions from the guide and relevant knowledge references, with citations that resolve to real sections, so answers are grounded in published material rather than free-floating model output.
- An operations scoring capability lets an operator assess how their environment measures up against the guide's definition of good.

Isvara is a companion project to the Architecture to Autonomy blog: the design philosophy behind it — an agentic assistant that reads a large operations guide directly from context, deliberately without a database or vector store — is discussed on the blog.
